contribution.question: Your notes say what the team did. What did you do yourself, especially when the jobs started failing in week 9?
contribution.why: The form asks for your individual contribution, and every sentence in your notes describes the team.

answer.text: For our final-year group project, four of us built a self-service GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster.
Students submitted training jobs through a web form, and the runner queued them on Kubernetes (k3s) across six lab workstations with GPUs.
We used Python and FastAPI for the API, Redis for the queue, Helm charts for deployment, and Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.
Our main technical decision was to use Kubernetes Jobs with a scheduler extender instead of Slurm: the department wanted every workload in a container, and we needed GPU quotas per course.
I wrote that per-course quota check in the scheduler extender.
In week 9, jobs started being OOMKilled at random, even with tiny models.
I found the cause by reading dmesg on the nodes: /dev/shm defaulted to 64 MB, which crashed the PyTorch data loaders.
I wrote the Helm change that mounts a memory-backed emptyDir with a size limit for each job, which fixed it.
The lesson was to check the node's kernel log first: we lost two days before looking.
In the spring term 140 students used the runner, and the average wait for a GPU fell from about two days on the old sign-up sheet to under 20 minutes.

letter.text: I am applying for the Graduate Cloud Platform Engineer 2027 role in Bristol.
In my final-year group project, four of us built a self-service GPU job runner for our department's machine learning teaching cluster, running on Kubernetes across six lab workstations.
When jobs started dying in week 9, I traced the failures through dmesg to a 64 MB /dev/shm and wrote the Helm change that fixed them.
I also wrote the per-course quota check in our scheduler extender.
By the spring term, 140 students were using it, and the average wait for a GPU had fallen from about two days to under 20 minutes.

I enjoyed the infrastructure side of that project more than the machine learning side, and Graphcore builds both the hardware and the cloud platform that models run on, which is why this role appeals to me.
Thank you for considering my application.
